newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore's rulers raise election stakes.
newsitem.headline: Singapore's rulers raise election stakes.

text.p: Singapore's People's Action Party (PAP), firmly entrenched in government, has raised the stakes for voters in the looming general elections by treating them as a "local election", analysts said on Tuesday.
They said the change in strategy came from the PAP's belief that the issues which concerned most voters are parochial "bread and butter issues", not the national issues it used to campaign on.
"I think it would probably work," said neutral constituional lawyer Kevin Tan.

"It panders to the lowest denominator. Those who do aspire for more idealistic goals are not going to see them realised because they are going to be swamped by all this talk about upgrading of housing estates."

Political analyst and lawyer Shriniwas Rai described the January 2 elections, in which the PAP is assured of 47 seats in the 83-member parliament which the opposition is not contesting, as a "watershed" in Singapore's political development.

"The government has seized upon the psyche of Singaporeans. It would be a watershed in the sense that it will show exactly how people are going to think and what matters to them -- principles or their purse."
Analysts said both the PAP and the opposition were campaigning on the need to pass on more power to the people. But their strategies and objectives remained worlds apart.
As they did in the past, the opposition is campaigning on the need to build a "true democracy" to impose checks on the government and give more voice to ordinary folk.
The PAP is promising local communities and their members of parliament a greater say in running "local governments".
"This time from day one, whoever is in charge will have an impact on your life immediately," Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong told reporters on Monday.
Goh's vision is to evolve a "mini federal" system which he said will have more authority.
"In every constituency there will be a local government with a local programme and how you vote will affect immediately your own interest," Goh said.
Voting in the opposition would mean constituencies losing renovation and development programmes and "become slums", Goh added.
But Singapore Democractic Party (SDP) leader Chee Soon Juan said the opposition would stick to its guns and not be distracted by the PAP strategy.
"This election will not be hijacked by the PAP. It will not be a local election. It will be an election at the national level," he told a news conference on Monday.

National issues such as the high cost of living, coupled with an economic slowdown, an unpopular goods and services tax and high ministerial salaries required careful scrutiny through a greater opposition presence in parliament, said Workers Party leader J.B. Jeyaretnam.
"I have serious doubts about this whole idea of our opposition wards becoming slums because there is a problem in the allocation of funds," Tan said.
He and other analysts said renovation and development projects came from public money and should be seen as entitlements rather than privileges.

"If its to be seen as a privilege to be dished out by the party in power, you are exercising the rule of patronage," Tan said. "I think there is a very grave danger here because the PAP will then be subjecting itself to the same strategy that they have knocked all this time."
Rai said he did not believe this strategy would degenerate into "money politics.

"But it may allow for the development of political favours," he said. "You are tempting the electorate with a lot of these and if you can't offer anything then they would vote for somebody else...It would not help the (political) process."
